analysis.one_liner: Let regulators review large internet providers' data-cap and usage-based pricing to make sure charges were fairly based on cost.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to a House subcommittee and never advanced; no vote was ever taken before Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large internet service providers (those with 2 million or more subscribers) to file with the Federal Trade Commission before imposing tiered, usage-based pricing plans — the kind of plan that charges customers more as their data use rises. The FTC, working with the FCC, would have reviewed whether those charges were actually justified by the cost of providing service, held public hearings, and could have forced providers to change or drop plans that penalized consumers, with fines up to $1 million. It also would have covered nonprofits and colleges, not just households. The bill never left committee: it died there when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011, with no vote ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Household internet subscribers — including nonprofits and colleges — who would have been shielded from data caps and overage charges not justified by the provider's actual costs, especially heavy internet users such as people who stream video. Heavy users today often pay usage-based fees that bear little relation to the incremental cost of carrying their data.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residential broadband customers, especially heavy internet users

how_it_helps.text: It made it unlawful for large broadband providers to impose usage-based charges that were unjust, unreasonable, or unreasonably discriminatory, with the FTC empowered to suspend or revise such plans.

It required providers to prove in a public filing that tiered data charges were fairly based on the actual cost of service, and it required the FTC to hold public hearings in communities affected by a proposed plan.

It counted nonprofits and colleges as 'residential consumers' protected by the rules, and it specifically scrutinized whether usage charges penalized consumers for streaming video, the practice that had prompted cable companies to impose data caps to protect their cable TV revenue.

analysis.who_pays: Large broadband and cable companies (2 million+ subscribers), which would have faced cost-based review of their pricing plans, public hearings, possible fines up to $1 million, and restrictions on using data caps to protect their cable TV revenue from streaming-video competition.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have required large internet providers to submit detailed economic analyses of every tiered pricing plan and exposed them to fines of up to $1 million, which providers argued could discourage new service offerings and network investment.

The standard was broad: the FTC could reject any plan whose rates were not 'justified by the costs' of the network, a cost-based ratemaking approach that is difficult to administer and that critics of utility-style regulation say invites disputes over what network investments should count.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the upside was potentially significant: it targeted the practice of charging heavy internet users far more than the actual cost of carrying their data, precisely when cable companies had an incentive to punish cord-cutters. The drawbacks: the bill would have inserted the FTC into detailed rate regulation of internet pricing, with mandatory filings, hearings, and penalties that could slow the rollout of new service tiers or raise compliance costs; some economists argue usage-based pricing is a legitimate way to manage network congestion and fund infrastructure, and a blanket "unjust and unreasonable" standard gave regulators wide discretion. The bill never advanced far enough for these tradeoffs to be tested in hearings.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to a House committee and then a subcommittee, sat there with no hearings or vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 16, 2009 by Rep. Eric Massa and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where it stayed; the action history shows no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote.
No further action appears before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill never received a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major broadband and cable companies, which faced no limit on data caps or usage-based pricing; consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Cable and broadband companies, free to impose data caps

for.name: Reps. Tom Perriello and Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Joined Massa as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup, and it died there.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican supported it, but no floor or committee vote was ever held, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have subjected large providers' usage-based pricing (data caps and overage fees) to cost-based FTC review, capping their ability to charge heavy users well above cost. Data caps were also a way to protect cable TV revenue from customers switching to streaming video.
